rows.source: HSE gas-network safety management
rows.verified: The Gas Safety (Management) Regulations cover safe management of natural-gas flow through networks supplying domestic and other consumers.

rows.source: HSE gas-network safety management
rows.verified: The regulations require arrangements to minimise the risk of a gas supply emergency.

rows.source: HSE gas-network safety management
rows.verified: The regulations require arrangements for dealing with supply emergencies, reported gas escapes and gas incidents.

rows.source: HSE gas-network safety management
rows.verified: A gas conveyor must have an HSE-accepted safety case before conveying gas through a network.

rows.source: HSE gas-network safety management
rows.verified: Where multiple gas transporters operate on one network, there must be a sole network emergency co-ordinator with an accepted safety case.

rows.source: HSE gas-network safety management
rows.verified: Each gas network must have an emergency reporting service provider able to receive public reports of gas escapes.

rows.source: HSE gas-network safety management
rows.verified: A gas supply emergency can arise when reduced network pressure creates danger through incomplete combustion, extinguished flames, fire or explosion.

rows.source: HSE gas-network safety management
rows.verified: Gas industry participants and relevant consumers must co-operate where necessary to maintain safe network pressure and minimise supply-emergency risk.

rows.source: HSE gas-network safety management
rows.verified: Gas-network risk depends on pressure, demand and supply balance, network configuration, gas composition, equipment, emergency arrangements and dutyholder co-operation.

rows.source: HSE gas-network safety management
rows.verified: HSE gas-supply evidence is network-, operator-, emergency-, consumer-, equipment- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level fire or exposure probability.

rows.source: UKHSA, Defra and APHA brucellosis control
rows.verified: Brucellosis affects several animal species, including cattle, sheep, goats and pigs, and can also infect humans.

rows.source: UKHSA, Defra and APHA brucellosis control
rows.verified: Brucellosis is a notifiable animal disease and suspected disease must be reported immediately to the relevant authority.

rows.source: UKHSA, Defra and APHA brucellosis control
rows.verified: Human symptoms can include fever, headache, muscle and joint pain and extreme tiredness.

rows.source: UKHSA, Defra and APHA brucellosis control
rows.verified: Human infection may follow contact with infected placenta or genital discharge from animals.

rows.source: UKHSA, Defra and APHA brucellosis control
rows.verified: Humans can also acquire infection by consuming raw milk or dairy products made from infected milk.

rows.source: UKHSA, Defra and APHA brucellosis control
rows.verified: Strict farm biosecurity is an important preventive measure, particularly when handling aborted foetuses and birth material.

rows.source: UKHSA, Defra and APHA brucellosis control
rows.verified: APHA investigates reported abortions and may test animals or milk as part of surveillance and control.

rows.source: UKHSA, Defra and APHA brucellosis control
rows.verified: The UKHSA Brucella Reference Unit provides diagnostic testing and advice on clinical management.

rows.source: UKHSA, Defra and APHA brucellosis control
rows.verified: Brucellosis risk depends on animal species, herd status, exposure to birth material, food practices, occupation, laboratory confirmation and control timing.

rows.source: UKHSA, Defra and APHA brucellosis control
rows.verified: Official brucellosis evidence is animal-, herd-, food-, person-, laboratory- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level infection probability.
